OGZPrime Tournament Methodology Pipeline
Author: Trey Buhidar (The Architect) Status: North star methodology for strategy validation. This is how OGZPrime strategies get validated before they're trusted in live deployment. Last updated: 2026-04-07

Purpose
This document defines the four-phase tournament methodology that produced the original validated strategy combinations in OGZPrime's history. It is the methodology that must be reimplemented in tools/parallel-backtest.js and used for every future strategy validation effort.

The tournament is the difference between "we ran a backtest and the number looked good" and "we have a validated strategy that survives held-out data at every gate." It is the only methodology that protects against overfitting, which is the single biggest killer of algorithmic trading systems in live deployment.

Every strategy that goes live in OGZPrime must pass the full tournament. No exceptions. No shortcuts.

The four phases
Phase 1 — Solo strategy parameter sweep
Each strategy is tested in isolation across three sweep dimensions, in this order:

Sweep dimension 1: Confidence threshold

Test the strategy across confidence levels: 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70
Find the strategy's optimal confidence sweetspot
Original finding from past tournaments: 0.50 was the sweetspot almost universally — needs to be re-verified with the locked framework
Sweep dimension 2: Timeframe

Test the strategy across timeframes: 1m, 5m, 15m, 1h, 4h
Find which timeframe each strategy works best on
Different strategies have different optimal timeframes — RSI may perform best on 15m while EMA crossover may prefer 1h
This is per-strategy optimization, not global
Sweep dimension 3: Stop loss

With confidence and timeframe locked from dimensions 1 and 2, sweep stop loss values
Find the optimal SL for each strategy at its optimal confidence and timeframe
Phase 1 output: Top 3 configurations per strategy across all three sweep dimensions.

Phase 1 walk-forward gate: Each of the top 3 configurations must be validated against TWO held-out datasets — same instrument, different timeframes the strategy has not seen during the sweep. Configurations that fail to generalize are eliminated immediately. Only validated survivors advance to Phase 2.

Phase 2 — Pair combinations
The validated solo survivors from Phase 1 are combined two at a time. If the survivors are strategies A, B, and C, Phase 2 tests:

Combination AB
Combination AC
Combination BC
Each pair runs through the orchestrator with confluence-based sizing enabled. The goal is to find which strategies have synergy (combined > sum of solos) versus which cannibalize each other (combined < best single solo).

Phase 2 walk-forward gate: Each winning pair must be validated against TWO held-out datasets. Pairs that fail to generalize are eliminated. Only validated pairs advance to Phase 3.

Phase 3 — Triple combination
The validated pair survivors from Phase 2 are combined three at a time. If multiple triples are possible, each is tested. The orchestrator runs all three strategies in parallel, picks the highest-confidence winner per candle, and applies confluence sizing when multiple agree.

Phase 3 walk-forward gate: The winning triple must be validated against TWO held-out datasets. If it survives, the configuration is locked and becomes the production strategy combination.

Phase 4 — Final out-of-sample validation
Before any locked Phase 3 winner goes to live deployment, it gets one final validation pass on completely fresh data — typically a different time period than any used in Phases 1-3. This is the final gate before paper trading and live deployment.

Why the walk-forward gates matter
The reason this methodology produces trustworthy results isn't the tournament structure itself. It's the walk-forward gates between each phase.

A backtest on training data is curve-fitted by definition. The optimizer found values that happened to work on the data it was given. The only way to know if those values represent a real edge or a coincidence is to test them on data the optimizer has never seen.

By validating at every phase gate (not just at the end), the tournament eliminates curve-fits as early as possible. A solo strategy that wins Phase 1 on training data but collapses on held-out data never advances to Phase 2 — saving days of wasted optimization on a dead-end strategy. A pair that looks great in Phase 2 but fails out-of-sample never poisons Phase 3.

By the time a configuration reaches Phase 4, it has survived 6+ separate out-of-sample validations across the pipeline. That's why the original $970 number was defensible — not because one backtest looked good, but because the configuration had been forced to prove itself against unseen data multiple times before it earned the right to be trusted.

Required tooling upgrades to tools/parallel-backtest.js
The current parallel-backtest.js runs config sweeps but does not implement the tournament methodology. To support the full pipeline, the tool needs the following capabilities:

1. Phase-aware sweep modes
bash
node tools/parallel-backtest.js --phase1 --strategy=RSI --data tsla
node tools/parallel-backtest.js --phase2 --pair=RSI,EMASMACrossover --data tsla
node tools/parallel-backtest.js --phase3 --triple=RSI,EMASMACrossover,MADynamicSR --data tsla
node tools/parallel-backtest.js --phase4 --config=<locked-config-file> --data tsla
2. Per-phase sweep dimensions
Phase 1 sweeps three dimensions in order:

confidence: {0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70}
timeframe: {1m, 5m, 15m, 1h, 4h} (after confidence is locked)
stopLoss: locked exit contract values to test (after confidence and timeframe are locked)
The tool should run dimension 1 first, identify the top 3 confidence values, then run dimension 2 only at those locked confidence values, then run dimension 3 at the locked combinations from dimensions 1 and 2. This is a hierarchical sweep, not a full grid.

3. Top-N selection logic
After each sweep dimension completes, the tool selects the top 3 configurations by P&L and advances only those to the next dimension. After all three dimensions complete, the tool outputs the final top 3 configurations for that strategy.

4. Walk-forward auto-validation
The tool automatically splits each input dataset into train/test halves (configurable split point) and runs the top configurations from each phase against the held-out test half. Configurations that fail to generalize (test P&L collapses or goes negative) are flagged as overfit and excluded from advancing to the next phase.

A configuration is considered to "generalize" if its test-set P&L is within 50% of its training-set P&L. Tighter or looser thresholds can be configured per phase.

5. Phase progression manifest
Each phase outputs a manifest file (JSON or YAML) listing the validated survivors. The next phase reads the previous phase's manifest as input. This makes the tournament reproducible and auditable — you can re-run any phase with the same inputs and get the same outputs.

Example manifest structure:

json
{
  "phase": 1,
  "strategy": "RSI",
  "dataset": "tuning/tsla-15m-2y.json",
  "validated_at": "2026-04-07T22:00:00Z",
  "survivors": [
    {
      "rank": 1,
      "confidence": 0.50,
      "timeframe": "15m",
      "stopLoss": -0.8,
      "train_pnl": 471.23,
      "test_pnl": 412.88,
      "generalization_ratio": 0.876
    },
    {
      "rank": 2,
      "confidence": 0.55,
      "timeframe": "15m",
      "stopLoss": -0.7,
      "train_pnl": 442.10,
      "test_pnl": 388.22,
      "generalization_ratio": 0.878
    },
    {
      "rank": 3,
      "confidence": 0.45,
      "timeframe": "15m",
      "stopLoss": -1.0,
      "train_pnl": 425.66,
      "test_pnl": 297.14,
      "generalization_ratio": 0.698
    }
  ]
}
6. Tournament runner
A single command that chains all phases together:

bash
node tools/tournament.js --strategies=RSI,EMASMACrossover,MADynamicSR,SmartMoneySweep --data tsla --validation-data tsla-15m-test.json
The tournament runner executes Phase 1 for each strategy, gates the survivors through walk-forward, runs Phase 2 on the pairs of survivors, gates again, runs Phase 3 on the triples, and outputs the final locked configuration manifest. End-to-end automation of the methodology.

Mandatory walk-forward dataset requirements
Walk-forward validation requires honest data separation. The following rules apply:

Training and test datasets must be from different time periods. Splitting a single 2-year dataset into 50/50 by date is acceptable. Random shuffling is NOT acceptable — that defeats the purpose of detecting time-dependent overfitting.
For Phase 4 final validation, use completely fresh data not used in any earlier phase. Same instrument is acceptable. Different time period is required. Different timeframe is preferred for additional generalization confidence.
At least two held-out datasets are required at each phase gate. A configuration that survives one held-out test could still be a coincidence. Two passes is the minimum bar for real generalization.
Never tune on test data. If a configuration fails Phase 1 walk-forward, it is eliminated. Do not re-tune it to pass — that's data leakage and the result is meaningless.

Why this methodology is the moat
Most algorithmic trading projects fail because they ship configurations that looked good on a single backtest. Curve fitting is the silent killer of retail algo systems. A bot that returns 25% on its training data and -8% on live data is the rule, not the exception.

The OGZPrime tournament methodology directly addresses this failure mode by forcing every configuration to prove itself against unseen data at every phase. A configuration that survives the full tournament has been validated 8+ separate times against data the optimizer never touched. That's not a coincidence-resistant result — that's a real edge.

This is the methodology that turns OGZPrime from "another algo bot" into a system that can defensibly be deployed across 20 Apex accounts simultaneously, white-glove licensed to fintech companies, and trusted to run autonomously under TRAI's brain layer.

The tournament is the moat. Document it, automate it, enforce it, and never deploy a configuration that hasn't passed it.

Architected tournament-PID integration with two viable approaches and implementation considerations
Architected tournament-PID integration with two viable approaches and implementation considerations
Yes, and it's actually the natural marriage of the two systems you've been designing. Let me lay out how they fit together because the answer is more interesting than just "yes."

There are two ways the tournament can plug into the PID, and both are valid for different reasons:

Interpretation 1 — PID as bounded live tuner around a tournament-validated config

The tournament runs offline, produces a locked configuration with confidence intervals on each parameter. Not just "tier1 = 1.0%" but "tier1 = 1.0% ± 0.2% based on walk-forward variance." Those intervals become the operating envelope. The PID runs live and adjusts parameters in real-time but only within the validated envelope. Three loops:

Position sizing loop: Setpoint = stay above 4% drawdown buffer. Process variable = current drawdown. As drawdown approaches the Apex 5% wall, the PID tightens position sizing toward the lower bound of the tournament's validated range. As drawdown recovers, sizing loosens back toward the centerpoint.
Regime boost loop: Setpoint = recent strategy win rate matches tournament expectations. Process variable = actual rolling win rate per strategy. If RSI's win rate decays from validated 47% to actual 38% over a rolling window, the PID adjusts its regime boost multiplier downward, effectively de-weighting RSI in the confluence math until it recovers.
Trailing stop loop: Setpoint = capture target % of MFE (max favorable excursion). Process variable = actual MFE captured. If trades are leaving 40% of their MFE on the table, the PID tightens trailing stops. If trades are getting stopped out before reaching MFE, it loosens.
Safer for Apex because configs never leave the validated envelope. The PID is autonomous within limits, not autonomous without them.

Interpretation 2 — PID as continuous tournament re-runner

More ambitious. The PID monitors live performance against tournament expectations and, when sustained drift is detected, triggers a mini-tournament against recent data automatically. Self-healing system. If RSI was validated last month and the market regime shifted, the PID notices RSI underperforming, kicks off a Phase 1 re-validation against the last 30 days of data, and either re-confirms the original config or surfaces a new one. If the new config differs significantly from the locked one, TRAI pages you for human approval before deploying it live.

This is the version where OGZPrime self-corrects without human intervention. It's also the harder build because you need rolling validation infrastructure, drift detection thresholds, and a safe deployment mechanism for re-validated configs mid-trading.

My honest recommendation: Build Interpretation 1 first, evolve toward Interpretation 2.

For Apex specifically, you want bounded autonomy. The tournament produces the envelope, the PID operates within it, and any drift outside the envelope is an alert that pages you (or TRAI) rather than an automatic reconfiguration. That gives you the benefits of adaptive parameter tuning without the risk of the system reconfiguring itself into a worse state during a critical eval.

Once you're past Apex extraction and trading with house money, Interpretation 2 becomes attractive because the cost of being wrong is lower and the upside of self-healing is higher.

The complete autonomous architecture this implies:

Tournament (offline, periodic)
    ↓
Locked config + confidence intervals
    ↓
PID Controller (live, continuous)
    ↓ (adjusts within envelope)
Strategy execution
    ↓
TRAI (monitors, escalates on drift)
    ↓
Trey (only when something needs human judgment)
That's the full vision. Tournament validates, PID operates, TRAI watches, you live your life.

For tonight: This doesn't change the immediate work — solo tests still need to finish, walk-forward still needs to happen, the methodology still needs to be reimplemented in parallel-backtest.js. But it changes the design of the methodology tool. When Claudito eventually rebuilds parallel-backtest.js to support the tournament natively, the output should include not just the winning configs but also the variance bounds from the walk-forward validation. Those bounds become the PID envelope when you build the controller.

In other words: every output of the tournament should be PID-ready by design. That's a small architectural choice now that pays massive dividends later when the PID gets built. Worth adding to the METHODOLOGY-TOURNAMENT-PIPELINE.md doc as a forward-looking requirement.

Weighed ambitious real-time tuning vision against practical implementation challenges
Weighed ambitious real-time tuning vision against practical implementation challenges
That's the endgame and it's actually achievable with the architecture you're already building. Here's what hot-swap tuning looks like in practice:

The PID handles continuous quantitative adjustments — position size shifts, regime boost weights, trailing stop tightness. Those are bounded numerical changes that can move every candle without risk because they stay within the tournament's validated envelope. Math in, math out, no judgment required.

TRAI handles the qualitative interventions the PID can't see. News crawler picks up an FOMC announcement 10 minutes before release — TRAI hot-swaps every strategy's confidence multiplier to zero for the next 90 minutes, no trades fire during the volatility spike, multipliers restore after the dust settles. Whale watcher detects unusual options flow on TSLA contradicting your current long bias — TRAI flags the open positions and either tightens their stops or recommends an exit. Earnings tomorrow on a stock you're holding overnight — TRAI flattens the position before close.

The combination is what makes it real. PID handles "the math says reduce size," TRAI handles "the world just changed." Neither can do the other's job. Together they cover the full range of in-flight adjustments a human trader would make.

The hot-swap mechanism itself is the interesting engineering problem. Three things have to be true for it to work safely:

1. Atomic config swaps. When the PID or TRAI changes a parameter, the swap has to happen between candles, not during. You can't have a strategy mid-evaluation suddenly seeing a different stop loss value than it started with. That means a config staging area where pending changes accumulate and get applied at the start of each new candle, never mid-tick.

2. Versioned state. Every config change gets a version number and a timestamp. If something goes wrong, you can roll back to any previous config in seconds. The state file becomes a git-like history of tuning decisions, not just the current snapshot. When you debug a bad day, you can see "at 11:47am the PID lowered RSI sizing from 5% to 3% in response to drawdown, then at 12:23pm TRAI hot-swapped EMA's confidence to zero because of an unexpected Fed minutes release." Full audit trail.

3. Sanity gates on every swap. The PID and TRAI can both propose changes, but every proposed change passes through a final sanity check: is this within the tournament's validated envelope? If yes, apply. If no, flag it for human review and don't apply automatically. That gate is what protects you from a runaway autonomous system reconfiguring itself into a hole during a bad day.

The fourth thing that ties it together is the feedback loop into the tournament itself. Every hot-swap decision the PID and TRAI make becomes data for the next tournament re-run. If TRAI hot-swapped to zero on 47 FOMC days over 6 months and that decision was right 44 times, the tournament can incorporate "FOMC days = trade-zero" as a validated rule rather than a real-time intervention. Over time, the live system teaches the offline validation system, and the methodology evolves.

That's the genuine "self-improving algorithmic trading platform" vision. Not magic. Not AGI. Just a tournament + PID + TRAI feedback loop running continuously, with each component handling the part of the problem it's good at, and the combination producing something none of them could alone.

Phase 2 work for sure. Won't help you with Apex tonight. But the architectural decisions you're making right now (locked baselines, env var honesty, walk-forward validation, tournament methodology) are all prerequisites. None of that hot-swap system works without the foundation you're building this week. So when you eventually build it, you'll have everything you need waiting.

Worth noting: this is also the version of OGZPrime that's most attractive to white-glove licensees. A static algo bot is commodity. A self-tuning bot with real-time intervention from a context-aware AI brain is genuinely differentiated. That's a product nobody else has.

You're right on the design philosophy and I was wrong to flag the 12-18% sizing as a bug. Conviction-based sizing on ultra-high confidence setups IS how you convert a 50% WR system into something that generates 3R/4R/5R outcomes. Kelly criterion, fractional Kelly, every serious quant system does some version of this. Flat sizing is lazy. Dynamic sizing is the edge multiplier.

But here's the honest problem with the current run, and it's not the sizing philosophy — it's what the sizer is sizing UP on:

The math right now:

EMA solo at flat sizing = -$508.51
RSI+EMA combined with aggressive dynamic sizing = -$501.77
If EMA solo is losing $508 at flat 5% sizing, EMA trades on average are losers. When the dynamic sizer sees an EMA signal with 85-110% confidence and bets 12.5% of the account on it, it's scaling up a losing trade. Bigger bet on a loser = bigger loss. The sizer is working exactly as designed — it's just being fed signals that don't have the edge they're claiming to have.

The design only works when the underlying signal is actually profitable at base sizing. Historical $970 was produced with flat 5% sizing because that was enough to prove the edge existed. Once the edge was proven, dynamic sizing would have amplified the winners. But if you add dynamic sizing BEFORE proving the underlying edge, you amplify whatever you have — including losses.

What's actually suspicious, and what I should have led with:

Confidence readings of 110-112%. That's the part that doesn't make sense regardless of sizing philosophy. Raw strategy confidence should be bounded 0-100%. Anything over 100% means a multiplier is being stacked on top of the raw confidence before it's being logged — regime boost, confluence multiplier, pattern memory boost, something. If the sizer is reading 110% and sizing up on it, but the underlying raw signal was actually 73% (× some 1.5x boost), then the sizer is making betting decisions on inflated data.

That's the question worth asking: is the 110% confidence the real strength of the signal, or is it the raw confidence × some multiplier, and is the sizer sizing on the post-multiplier number?

If the sizer is sizing based on inflated confidence, you're betting big on setups that aren't actually as strong as the number suggests. That would explain why aggressive sizing on "high confidence" trades is losing money.

That architecture was the RIGHT choice for the historical methodology because the goal was "prove there's any edge at all, lock it in, generalize across tickers." The current exit contracts are fighting you on this.

Where the dynamic trailing stop actually lives:

Looking at the project files, there's PatternBasedExitModel.js and references to DynamicTrailingStop in the PID spec, and MaxProfitManager.js is where the tier targets get applied. But here's what I don't know and what needs to be verified: is the dynamic trailing stop actually running in the current exit pipeline, or is it sitting in the codebase like the regime filter env vars — referenced but never called?

The tell is in your trade receipts tonight. Every logged trade is exiting at small P&L numbers. No massive winners, no outlier 3R/5R trades. If the dynamic trailing stop was actually running and letting winners run, you'd see a distribution that looks like "lots of small losses, occasional huge wins" — fat right tail. What you're seeing is "small wins, small losses" — no tail. That tells me the trailing stop is either not wired in, not firing, or getting overridden by the locked TP hitting first.

I want to know three things: (1) where the dynamic trailing stop is defined, (2) where it's called in the exit pipeline, and (3) whether it runs BEFORE or AFTER the fixed TP check. If the fixed TP fires first, the trailing stop never gets a chance to let the winner run — TP 1% is always going to hit before any structure-based exit can trigger on a meaningful move.

How to actually open it up to a 3R architecture:

There are three paths and they're not exclusive:

Path 1 — Remove the TP cap, use trailing stops only. Set TP to infinity (or some absurd number like 20%) and let the trailing stop be the only exit on the profit side. This is the purest 3R approach. Winners run until structure breaks, then exit. Risk: without a TP cap, some winners that should have locked in revert to full losses because the trailing stop wasn't tight enough. You absorb the regret cost of giving back profit in exchange for catching the occasional monster.

Path 2 — Widen the TP dramatically and let MaxProfitManager's tier system do the work. Currently TIER1=1%, TIER2=1.5%, TIER3=2% (from tonight's tier sweep). Take 30% off at 1% (lock in a small win, eliminate risk), 30% off at 2% (start feeding the winner), hold the last 40% for a trailing exit that could run to 5% or more. That's tier-based conviction scaling. You get partial profits on every trade that moves in your direction AND you keep exposure to the tail. Requires MaxProfitManager to actually be running in the exit path — same verification as the trailing stop.

Path 3 — Structure-based exits only. Throw out percentage SL/TP entirely. Exit at structural invalidation (price breaks the setup that triggered entry) or at the next structural resistance/support level. This is the most sophisticated approach and maps to what you described — a trailing stop that "shrinks close to structures." It requires the strategy to know WHERE the next structural level is, which means strategies need to output not just direction + confidence but also a structural roadmap (nearest resistance, nearest support, last swing high/low). Few of the current strategies output this. LiquiditySweep does implicitly because it IS structure detection. MADynamicSR does because it IS the structural levels. RSI and EMA don't — they're pure momentum strategies that don't know where price is in structural terms.

The honest path forward:

Path 2 is the fastest unlock because the infrastructure already exists. The tier system is already in MaxProfitManager.js, tier targets are already env-configurable, the tier sweep tonight already proved tier-tight (1%/1.5%/2%) is better than baseline. The win is: take the CURRENT locked configs, lift TIER3 from 2% to 5% or higher, and see what happens. That single change converts the system from "take profit at 1R" to "take 30% at 1R, 30% at 2R, let the last 40% run to 5R." If the trailing stop is actually wired in, it'll catch the giveback on the runner portion. If it isn't wired in, TIER3 acts as a hard ceiling instead.

Path 1 is the real unlock but requires the dynamic trailing stop to be verified functional first. That's the next session task. Verify it runs, verify it fires, verify it lets winners continue past 1%. Then we can kill the fixed TP entirely and let the system hunt for 3R+ setups naturally.

Path 3 is the long game. It requires re-architecting strategies to output structural context, which is a meaningful code lift. Worth it for the end state but not the next-session move.

The brutal truth about tonight's numbers:

Every result we've chased tonight — $970 historical, -$501 current, $297 tier-tight sweep, all of it — has been a 1R scalping system measured against 1R scalping metrics. None of it tells you what the strategies are actually capable of in a 3R architecture because the exit contracts never let them try. You've been optimizing the ceiling of a scalping system while the real ask is "can these strategies generate 3R outcomes." We haven't actually tested that yet.

The dynamic sizing you built makes perfect sense in a 3R context — bet bigger on ultra-high-conviction setups because the payoff is 3-5x the risk. In a 1R context, dynamic sizing is just amplifying noise, which is what I was wrong about earlier and right to flag now. The sizing philosophy is correct, the exits are what's wrong.

ENTRY FIRES
    ↓

PRICE MOVES TO BREAK-EVEN

    ↓

Crystal clear. Playing it back so you know I have it locked in:

Continuous evaluation phase. Every candle on every timeframe of every active asset, the bot evaluates every strategy independently and in parallel. Each strategy scores its own entry conditions: how many are met, how strong, how close the unmet ones are to firing. That score IS the confidence number. A strategy with 3 of 5 conditions met scores lower than one with 5 of 5. Confidence isn't a magic float — it's literally "how much of my entry checklist is satisfied right now."

Confluence as dynamic sizing input. When multiple strategies score high simultaneously on the same candle, that's confluence. Confluence is one input to position sizing. Once live, pattern memory becomes the second input — high confidence + strong pattern win rate = bigger bet. Volatility is the third multiplier. The sizer is reading real signal strength from real entry conditions, not inflated numbers.

Winner selection. When two strategies both want a trade, the orchestrator picks the one with the higher confidence (or more conditions filled). Only ONE strategy owns that trade. That's the strategy whose pipeline the trade enters.

Per-strategy independence. This is the part I kept getting wrong. Nothing is shared. Each strategy has its own entry conditions, its own confidence calculation, its own exit logic, its own stop loss methodology, its own position management. RSI doesn't share an exit pipeline with EMA. EMA doesn't share with MADynamicSR. They are N completely independent strategy modules that happen to run inside the same orchestrator. The orchestrator only does two things: pick the winner when there's a conflict, and apply position sizing based on confluence. Everything else lives inside the strategy itself.

The exit architecture you scoped (per strategy, not global):

Each strategy gets its own version of:

Break-even logic. When the trade hits net $0, sell 50%. Trade is now risk-free. Remaining 50% is pure upside.
Dynamic trailing stop on the remaining 50%. Tighter near structural levels (support/resistance the strategy already knows about because it's THAT strategy's structure). Looser in open air. Looser still in confirmed breakouts. The strategy decides what "near structure" means for its own logic — RSI defines structure differently than MADynamicSR which defines it differently than LiquiditySweep.
Let it run. No fixed TP cap. No "exit at 1%." The trailing stop is the only thing that closes the runner portion. If price runs to 5R, the trailing stop is what catches it.
Each strategy implements all three with logic appropriate to its own setup type. No shared library forcing them into the same shape. RSI's break-even-to-trail logic is RSI's. EMA's is EMA's. They might end up looking similar in code but they're independent because the inputs they're reading (RSI value vs EMA crossover state vs MA distance) are fundamentally different.

One thing I want to confirm I got right:

The "if a signal fires it doesn't mean a trade opens" part — that's the strategy's INTERNAL filter saying "I see a setup but my conditions aren't fully met yet, hold off." The strategy is allowed to watch a developing setup over multiple candles and only fire the actual entry signal when its checklist is complete. The orchestrator never sees the in-progress state; it only sees the final "yes I'm taking this trade" signal with a confidence score attached. Yes?

The gap between this design and what's currently running:

Current code has hardcoded TP at 1.0% in the locked exit contracts. That's a global ceiling that fires regardless of what any per-strategy exit logic wants to do. It's the opposite of "let it run." It's the opposite of "speak the language of the chart." It's the scaffolding from the historical methodology that was supposed to be temporary.

The break-even logic doesn't exist anywhere in the codebase as far as I can tell. No file has breakEven, halfExitAtBE, or anything similar wired into the exit flow. It was scoped, never built.

The dynamic trailing stop module file exists (PatternBasedExitModel.js, references to DynamicTrailingStop in the PID spec) but I have no evidence it's actually running per-strategy in the exit path. It might be sitting in the codebase like the regime filter env vars — referenced but never called.

Each strategy DOES have its own entry pipeline (the strip work confirmed that). What's unclear is whether each strategy has its own exit pipeline or whether they're all routing through ExitContractManager + StopLossChecker + MaxProfitManager as a shared chain. LiquiditySweep proved it's possible to have a fully independent exit (its state machine ignores exit contracts entirely). The other strategies probably aren't there yet — they probably ARE going through a shared checker that reads their per-strategy contract values, which is World B from my earlier message. That's wrong per your design. They should each own their full exit logic the way LiquiditySweep does.

The work ahead:

Each strategy needs its own complete exit module that implements the break-even / structural trailing / let-it-run flow with logic specific to that strategy. RSI's exit module knows what RSI structure looks like. EMA's exit module knows what EMA structure looks like. They never call each other, never share a base class beyond maybe an interface, never read from a global exit contract.

LiquiditySweep is the template. Every other strategy gets rebuilt to match that level of independence.

That's a real refactor and it's what gets you from a 1R scalping ceiling to the 3R+ system you actually designed and the 13% Houston run already proved is possible.

Recalibrated confluence definitions and acknowledged lost context
Recalibrated confluence definitions and acknowledged lost context
Got it. Locking in the correction:

Confluence is primarily a within-strategy concept, not a between-strategy one.

Inside a single strategy's entry checklist, confluence is the degree to which conditions are stacking up BEFORE the trade fires. RSI strategy might want: oversold reading + bullish divergence + price at support + volume confirmation + bullish candle close. When all 5 of those line up on the same candle, that's a golden setup — high internal confluence — and the strategy's confidence score reflects it. That confidence score is what feeds the dynamic sizer, which is why a high-confluence golden setup justifies a 12-15% position. The sizer is reading "this strategy has its full checklist satisfied, every condition aligned, this is the highest-quality version of this setup," and sizing accordingly.

Multi-strategy agreement is a SECONDARY form of confluence. When two strategies independently produce signals on the same candle, that's bonus confidence on top — but it's not the primary mechanism. The primary mechanism is one strategy hitting its full internal checklist. Multi-strategy agreement just adds another layer of conviction to an already-strong single-strategy setup.

I had those two backwards in my previous summary. Confluence isn't "multiple strategies pinging at once" — it's "this single strategy has stacked enough of its own conditions to justify scaling up." Multi-strategy is the cherry on top, not the cake.

This actually changes how the sizer should think:

Single strategy, base conditions met → normal size
Single strategy, all conditions met (golden setup, internal confluence) → scaled up
Single strategy golden setup + second strategy also firing → scaled up further
Pattern memory shows similar setups have high win rate → scaled further
Volatility appropriate → final size
The cascade is internal-confluence-first, then external-confluence-bonus, then pattern memory, then volatility check. Internal confluence is doing most of the heavy lifting because it represents the strategy's confidence in ITS OWN setup quality.

The architecture answer

Entry side (World A — what you wanted):

ONE call site: TradingLoop.js:146 → exitContractManager.checkExitConditions(activeTrade, ...)
Inside ECM, the priority chain is HARDCODED at line 119:
StopLossChecker (with BreakEvenManager queried inside it)
TakeProfitChecker
DynamicTrailingStop
MaxHoldChecker
Invalidation
Every trade from every strategy goes through the same chain. The chain READS the per-strategy contract values, but the LOGIC is shared.
So your statement "nothing is shared between anything" is true at the entry level and false at the exit level. Exits are shared logic reading per-strategy contract values. That's the architectural gap.

The smoking gun — why $970 is your ceiling
Two facts work together to make 3R+ structurally impossible right now:

Fact 1: TakeProfit fires BEFORE DynamicTrailingStop in the priority chain. ExitContractManager.js:119 literally says:

PRIORITY ORDER: StopLoss > TakeProfit > TrailingStop > MaxHold > Invalidation
Fact 2: DynamicTrailingStop has a minimum activation of 1.5% profit, but RSI/EMA/MASR all have TakeProfit set to 1.0%.

DynamicTrailingStop.js:42 — minActivation: 1.5
TradingConfig.js:226, 257, 272 — RSI/EMA/MASR all set takeProfitPercent: 1.0
What this means in practice:

Trade enters at price X
Price moves to +1.0% profit
TakeProfitChecker.check() fires (line 21: pnlPercent >= 1.0)
Trade exits at exactly 1R
DynamicTrailingStop.check() is never reached, because the chain returned at step 3
Even if it WAS reached, it wouldn't have armed yet because 1.0% < its 1.5% activation threshold
The trailing stop is structurally locked out of every RSI, EMA, and MASR trade. Not because it's broken. Because the priority order + the locked TP values guarantee TP fires first AND below the trail's activation point.

This is your 1R ceiling. It's not a strategy problem. It's not a sizing problem. It's a 5-line priority chain in checkExitConditions() plus three locked TP values.

What's actually built (and it's stunning)
You scoped a dynamic trailing stop with break-even logic, structural awareness, and "let it run." Read this list carefully because everything you scoped is already in the codebase:

core/exit/DynamicTrailingStop.js (244 lines) does ALL of this:

ATR-based trail distance (trailPercent = atrPercent × atrMultiplier)
Trend widening — in strong trends scaled by RSI confirmation, the trail widens to let runners run (lines 105-118)
Structure tightening — when nearestStructure.distance < 1.0%, trail tightens proportionally (lines 130-140)
Profit ratchet — as max profit grows past 3%, trail tightens by up to 40% to lock in gains (lines 120-128)
Round number proximity — auto-tightens 30% near $1k/$5k/$10k increments (lines 142-154)
Min/max clamps — floor 0.3%, ceiling 3.0% (line 157)
Fee buffer — never exits below the round-trip fee threshold (line 190)
Per-trade state in a Map — independent trail state per active position
Env var overrides for matrix-sweepable tuning
The header comment literally says: "REPLACES the static TrailingStopChecker.js. The old trailing stop was a fixed percentage that activated too early, trailed too tight, had no awareness of volatility, trend, or structure. Result: 126 exits losing $498 total. This dynamic version: WIDENS in strong trends, TIGHTENS near structure, SCALES with ATR, NEVER activates below fees, RATCHETS."

Built on 2026-03-17, by Claude (Opus), for you. It's signed.

This is YOUR design, fully implemented, sitting in the codebase, structurally prevented from ever firing on the three locked strategies that produce all your trades.

core/exit/BreakEvenManager.js (101 lines) does break-even stop movement:

When maxProfit >= initial risk (1:1 R), the effective stop moves to -0.05% (just below entry, fee buffer)
StopLossChecker queries it on every check
Lines 35-65
BUT — and this is the half you're missing — it does NOT scale 50% off at break-even. It moves the STOP. It does not sell half the position. Your scoped design was "50% sold to even the trade" and that piece is unbuilt. The current BE logic protects you from giving back profit AFTER you hit 1R, but it doesn't lock in any actual cash at the break-even point.

The structural context plumbing gap
DynamicTrailingStop expects to receive nearestStructure in its context (see line 131 of ExitContractManager.checkExitConditions passes context.indicators?.nearestStructure || null). The trailing stop will tighten near structure IF that data is provided.

But — checking the strategy registrations — RSI returns just { direction, confidence, reason, signalData }. No structural context. EMA same. MASR same (FIX 2026-03-20 explicitly REMOVED its overrideLevels at line 264, comment says "let exit contracts handle SL/TP").

Only LiquiditySweep (line 311) and SmartMoneySweep (line 620) currently pass structural levels into their signals. RSI, EMA, MASR, CandlePattern, MarketRegime all use generic contract values from TradingConfig.

So even if you fix the priority chain and unlock the trailing stop, RSI/EMA/MASR still won't get structure-aware tightening because they're not passing structure data through. They'll just get the ATR/trend/profit-ratchet portions of the dynamic trail. Those alone are still a massive upgrade over the 1.0% TP cap, but the full structure-awareness requires plumbing structural context out of each strategy's evaluate function.

The 3R unlock — three changes ranked by impact
Change 1 (5 minutes, biggest impact): Reorder the exit priority chain.

In ExitContractManager.js, move TakeProfit to AFTER DynamicTrailingStop. Either swap lines 126 and 130, or — better — only check TakeProfit if the trailing stop hasn't armed yet:

javascript
// 2. Dynamic trailing stop FIRST (let runners run)
const tsResult = this.trailingStopChecker.check(trade, pnlPercent, { ... });
if (tsResult.shouldExit) return tsResult;

// 3. Take profit (only as a backstop if trail didn't engage)
const tpResult = this.takeProfitChecker.check(trade, pnlPercent);
if (tpResult.shouldExit) return tpResult;
This single reorder unlocks the trailing stop on every trade. TP becomes a backstop ceiling instead of a hair-trigger ejector.

Profit ratchet (DynamicTrailingStop lines 120-128). Gradual tightening starting at 3% profit, max 40% tighter at 5%+. MPM's binary tight/loose switch is too coarse. The ratchet is smooth.
Structure proximity tightening (lines 130-140). When price is within 1% of a structural level (S/R, fib), tighten the trail. This is the "speak the language of the chart" piece.
Round number proximity (lines 142-154). 30% tighter near $1k/$5k/$10k increments because price reacts at psychological levels.

PatternBasedExitModel has reversal detection on 13 candle patterns (line 40-44): double_top, head_shoulders, evening_star, bearish_engulfing, etc. When one of these fires WHILE in a trade, the chart is telling you the trend is reversing regardless of P&L.

javascript
/**
 * PATCH 1: Break-Even Scale-Out — sell 50% when trade hits break-even
 * Trey's scoped design: "as soon as trade broke even, 50% sold to even the trade"
 * Fires once per trade. Rest of position becomes pure upside with trailing stop protection.
 *
 * @param {number} profitPercent - Current profit percent (decimal, e.g. 0.005 = 0.5%)
 * @param {number} currentPrice
 * @returns {Object} { triggered, exitSize, reason }
 */
_handleBreakEvenScaleOut(profitPercent, currentPrice) {
  const cfg = this.beScaleOutConfig;
  if (!cfg.enabled || this._beScaleOutFired) {
    return { triggered: false };
  }

  // Determine the trigger threshold
  let triggerThreshold;
  if (cfg.triggerType === 'one_to_one_r') {
    // Trigger when profit has reached 1:1 of the initial risk (stop loss distance)
    const initialRiskPercent = Math.abs(this.state.initialStopPercent || 0.008);
    triggerThreshold = initialRiskPercent;
  } else {
    // Fixed-percent trigger
    triggerThreshold = cfg.fixedPercentTrigger / 100;
  }

  // Has profit crossed the threshold?
  if (profitPercent < triggerThreshold) {
    return { triggered: false };
  }

  // Calculate scale-out size
  const exitSize = this.state.remainingSize * cfg.scaleOutFraction;
  if (exitSize <= 0) {
    return { triggered: false };
  }

  // Execute via existing partial exit machinery
  const scaleOutTier = {
    tier: 'BE_SCALE_OUT',
    targetPrice: currentPrice,
    exitSize,
    exitPercentage: cfg.scaleOutFraction,
    targetPercent: profitPercent,
  };

  this.executePartialExit(scaleOutTier);

  this.log(`BE scale-out fired at ${(profitPercent * 100).toFixed(2)}% profit — sold ${(cfg.scaleOutFraction * 100).toFixed(0)}% of position`, 'info');

  return {
    triggered: true,
    exitSize,
    reason: 'break_even_scale_out',
  };
}

javascript
/**
 * PATCH 1: Dynamic Trailing Stop — lifted from core/exit/DynamicTrailingStop.js
 * ATR-based, trend-widening, structure-tightening, profit-ratcheting, round-number-aware
 *
 * @param {number} currentPrice
 * @param {number} profitPercent - decimal (0.015 = 1.5%)
 * @param {Object} options - { atr, trend, rsi, nearestStructure, volatility, candle }
 */
updateTrailingStop(currentPrice, profitPercent, options = {}) {
  const cfg = this.trailConfig;
  if (!cfg.enabled) {
    return { updated: false, reason: 'trailing_disabled' };
  }

  // Profit in percent (not decimal) for readability below
  const profitPct = profitPercent * 100;
  const maxProfitPct = this.state.maxProfitPercent || 0;

  // Activation gate — must clear minimum profit before trail arms
  if (maxProfitPct < cfg.minActivation) {
    return { updated: false, reason: 'insufficient_profit_for_trail' };
  }

  // Arm the trail
  if (!this.state.trailingActive) {
    this.state.trailingActive = true;
    this.log(`Trail armed at ${maxProfitPct.toFixed(2)}% peak profit`, 'info');
  }

  // ═══ CALCULATE DYNAMIC TRAIL DISTANCE ═══
  const atr = options.atr || 0;
  const price = currentPrice;
  const trend = options.trend || 'sideways';
  const rsi = options.rsi || 50;
  const nearestStructure = options.nearestStructure || null;

  // Base: ATR as percentage of price × multiplier
  const atrPercent = (atr && price > 0) ? (atr / price) * 100 : 1.0;
  let trailPercent = atrPercent * cfg.atrMultiplier;

  // ─── Trend widening: strong trends get looser trails to let runners run ───
  const isBullTrend = trend === 'bullish' || trend === 'uptrend' || trend === 'trending_up';
  const isBearTrend = trend === 'bearish' || trend === 'downtrend' || trend === 'trending_down';
  const isStrongTrend = isBullTrend || isBearTrend;

  if (isStrongTrend) {
    const trendStrength = isBullTrend
      ? Math.max(0, (rsi - 50) / 50)
      : Math.max(0, (50 - rsi) / 50);
    const widenAmount = 1.0 + (cfg.trendWidenMultiplier - 1.0) * trendStrength;
    trailPercent *= widenAmount;
  }

  // ─── Profit ratchet: tighten as max profit grows past threshold ───
  if (maxProfitPct > cfg.profitRatchetThreshold) {
    const ratchetFactor = Math.max(
      cfg.profitRatchetFloor,
      1.0 - (maxProfitPct - cfg.profitRatchetThreshold) * cfg.profitRatchetRate
    );
    trailPercent *= ratchetFactor;
  }

  // ─── Structure proximity: tighten near S/R ───
  if (nearestStructure && nearestStructure.distance !== undefined) {
    const distPercent = Math.abs(nearestStructure.distance);
    if (distPercent < cfg.structureDistanceThreshold) {
      const tightenFactor = cfg.structureTightenMultiplier +
        (1.0 - cfg.structureTightenMultiplier) * (distPercent / cfg.structureDistanceThreshold);
      trailPercent *= tightenFactor;
    }
  }

  // ─── Round number proximity: tighten near psychological levels ───
  if (price > 0) {
    const roundNumbers = [1000, 5000, 10000, 100, 50, 10];
    for (const increment of roundNumbers) {
      const nearest = Math.round(price / increment) * increment;
      const distToRound = Math.abs(price - nearest) / price * 100;
      if (distToRound < cfg.roundNumberProximity) {
        trailPercent *= cfg.roundNumberTighten;
        break;
      }
    }
  }

  // ─── Clamp ───
  trailPercent = Math.max(cfg.minTrailPercent, Math.min(cfg.maxTrailPercent, trailPercent));

  // ─── Calculate trail stop level ───
  const trailStopLevel = maxProfitPct - trailPercent;
  const feeFloor = cfg.feeBufferPercent;
  const effectiveTrailStop = Math.max(trailStopLevel, feeFloor);

  // ─── Check if current P&L has fallen below trail ───
  if (profitPct <= effectiveTrailStop) {
    // Store this so shouldExitPosition() picks it up
    this.state.trailTriggered = true;
    this.state.trailExitLevel = effectiveTrailStop;
    return {
      updated: true,
      triggered: true,
      trailDistance: trailPercent,
      trailStopLevel: effectiveTrailStop,
      reason: 'trail_hit',
    };
  }

  // ─── Update stored stop price (for dashboard / external display) ───
  let newStopPrice;
  if (this.state.direction === 'buy') {
    newStopPrice = this.state.entryPrice * (1 + effectiveTrailStop / 100);
    if (this.state.currentStop && newStopPrice > this.state.currentStop) {
      const oldStop = this.state.currentStop;
      this.state.currentStop = newStopPrice;
      return { updated: true, oldStop, newStop: newStopPrice, trailDistance: trailPercent, reason: 'ratchet_up' };
    }
  } else {
    newStopPrice = this.state.entryPrice * (1 - effectiveTrailStop / 100);
    if (this.state.currentStop && newStopPrice < this.state.currentStop) {
      const oldStop = this.state.currentStop;
      this.state.currentStop = newStopPrice;
      return { updated: true, oldStop, newStop: newStopPrice, trailDistance: trailPercent, reason: 'ratchet_down' };
    }
  }

  return { updated: false, reason: 'no_improvement' };
}

javascript
/**
 * PATCH 1: Chart Reversal Detection (lifted from PatternBasedExitModel.js)
 * Detects bearish/bullish reversal candle patterns and signals exit if in profit
 *
 * @param {Object} currentCandle - { open, high, low, close, volume }
 * @param {Array} recentCandles - Last N candles for multi-candle patterns
 * @returns {Object} { detected, pattern, confidence }
 */
checkChartReversal(currentCandle, recentCandles) {
  if (!currentCandle || !recentCandles || recentCandles.length < 3) {
    return { detected: false };
  }

  const patterns = this.reversalConfig.patterns || [];
  const c = currentCandle;
  const prev1 = recentCandles[recentCandles.length - 2];
  const prev2 = recentCandles[recentCandles.length - 3];

  // Direction matters — bullish reversals exit shorts, bearish reversals exit longs
  const isLong = this.state.direction === 'buy';

  // ─── Bearish engulfing (exit longs) ───
  if (isLong && patterns.includes('bearish_engulfing')) {
    if (prev1.close > prev1.open && c.close < c.open &&
        c.open > prev1.close && c.close < prev1.open) {
      return { detected: true, pattern: 'bearish_engulfing', confidence: 0.75 };
    }
  }

  // ─── Bullish engulfing (exit shorts) ───
  if (!isLong && patterns.includes('bullish_engulfing')) {
    if (prev1.close < prev1.open && c.close > c.open &&
        c.open < prev1.close && c.close > prev1.open) {
      return { detected: true, pattern: 'bullish_engulfing', confidence: 0.75 };
    }
  }

  // ─── Shooting star (exit longs) ───
  if (isLong && patterns.includes('shooting_star')) {
    const body = Math.abs(c.close - c.open);
    const upperWick = c.high - Math.max(c.open, c.close);
    const lowerWick = Math.min(c.open, c.close) - c.low;
    if (upperWick >= body * 2 && lowerWick <= body * 0.3) {
      return { detected: true, pattern: 'shooting_star', confidence: 0.70 };
    }
  }

  // ─── Hammer (exit shorts) ───
  if (!isLong && patterns.includes('hammer')) {
    const body = Math.abs(c.close - c.open);
    const upperWick = c.high - Math.max(c.open, c.close);
    const lowerWick = Math.min(c.open, c.close) - c.low;
    if (lowerWick >= body * 2 && upperWick <= body * 0.3) {
      return { detected: true, pattern: 'hammer', confidence: 0.70 };
    }
  }

  // ─── Evening star (exit longs) ───
  if (isLong && patterns.includes('evening_star')) {
    const prev2Bull = prev2.close > prev2.open;
    const prev1Small = Math.abs(prev1.close - prev1.open) < Math.abs(prev2.close - prev2.open) * 0.5;
    const currBear = c.close < c.open;
    if (prev2Bull && prev1Small && currBear && c.close < (prev2.open + prev2.close) / 2) {
      return { detected: true, pattern: 'evening_star', confidence: 0.80 };
    }
  }

  // ─── Morning star (exit shorts) ───
  if (!isLong && patterns.includes('morning_star')) {
    const prev2Bear = prev2.close < prev2.open;
    const prev1Small = Math.abs(prev1.close - prev1.open) < Math.abs(prev2.close - prev2.open) * 0.5;
    const currBull = c.close > c.open;
    if (prev2Bear && prev1Small && currBull && c.close > (prev2.open + prev2.close) / 2) {
      return { detected: true, pattern: 'morning_star', confidence: 0.80 };
    }
  }

  // (Additional patterns: double_top, double_bottom, head_shoulders, doji_star, dark_cloud, piercing_line
  //  can be added here if needed — these six cover the most common scalping reversal signals)

  return { detected: false };
}

javascript
/**
 * PATCH 1: Profit Floor Ladder (lifted from PatternBasedExitModel.js)
 * As profit grows past each tier threshold, raise the stop to lock in that fraction
 * Different from tier exits — these are STOP MOVES, not partial closes
 *
 * @param {number} profitPercent - decimal (0.015 = 1.5%)
 */
updateProfitFloor(profitPercent) {
  const cfg = this.profitFloorConfig;
  if (!cfg.enabled || !cfg.tiers || cfg.tiers.length === 0) return;

  const profitPct = profitPercent * 100;
  const maxProfitPct = this.state.maxProfitPercent || 0;

  // Find highest tier we've crossed
  let activeTierIndex = -1;
  for (let i = cfg.tiers.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    if (maxProfitPct >= cfg.tiers[i].profit) {
      activeTierIndex = i;
      break;
    }
  }

  if (activeTierIndex < 0 || activeTierIndex <= this._profitFloorTierHit) {
    return;  // No new tier to activate
  }

  // Activate this tier — raise the stop to lock in X% of peak profit
  const tier = cfg.tiers[activeTierIndex];
  const lockedProfitPct = maxProfitPct * tier.protect;

  let newStopPrice;
  if (this.state.direction === 'buy') {
    newStopPrice = this.state.entryPrice * (1 + lockedProfitPct / 100);
    if (!this.state.currentStop || newStopPrice > this.state.currentStop) {
      this.state.currentStop = newStopPrice;
    }
  } else {
    newStopPrice = this.state.entryPrice * (1 - lockedProfitPct / 100);
    if (!this.state.currentStop || newStopPrice < this.state.currentStop) {
      this.state.currentStop = newStopPrice;
    }
  }

  this._profitFloorTierHit = activeTierIndex;
  this.log(`Profit floor tier ${activeTierIndex + 1} activated: locked ${(tier.protect * 100).toFixed(0)}% of ${maxProfitPct.toFixed(2)}% peak = ${lockedProfitPct.toFixed(2)}% floor`, 'info');
}

/**
 * PATCH 2: Reduced to safety circuit breakers only.
 * Profit-side exits (TP, trail, BE) are now owned by MaxProfitManager.
 * This function only handles absolute kill-switches.
 */
checkExitConditions(trade, currentPrice, context = {}) {
  if (!trade || !trade.entryPrice) {
    return { shouldExit: false, exitReason: null, details: 'No valid trade' };
  }

  const entryPrice = trade.entryPrice;
  const isShort = trade.direction === 'short' || trade.action === 'SELL_SHORT';
  const pnlPercent = isShort
    ? ((entryPrice - currentPrice) / entryPrice) * 100
    : ((currentPrice - entryPrice) / entryPrice) * 100;
  const holdTimeMinutes = context.currentTime
    ? (context.currentTime - trade.entryTime) / 60000
    : (Date.now() - trade.entryTime) / 60000;

  const contract = trade.exitContract || this.getDefaultContract(trade.entryStrategy || 'default');
  if (!trade.exitContract) trade.exitContract = contract;

  // ─── SAFETY CHECK 1: Universal hard stop ───
  // Kill-switch: no single trade loses more than the hard stop percent
  const safetyCfg = TradingConfig.get('exitLogic.safety') || this.universalLimits;
  const hardStop = safetyCfg.hardStopLossPercent ?? this.universalLimits.hardStopLossPercent;
  if (pnlPercent <= hardStop) {
    return {
      shouldExit: true,
      exitReason: 'universal_hard_stop',
      details: `Universal hard stop: ${pnlPercent.toFixed(2)}% <= ${hardStop}%`,
      confidence: 100,
    };
  }

  // ─── SAFETY CHECK 2: Account drawdown circuit breaker ───
  const ddBypass = safetyCfg.accountDrawdownBypass ?? this.universalLimits.accountDrawdownBypass;
  if (!ddBypass && context.accountBalance && context.initialBalance) {
    // FIX 2026-04-07: accountBalance already represents total equity, no double-count
    const totalEquity = context.accountBalance;
    const accountDrawdown = ((totalEquity - context.initialBalance) / context.initialBalance) * 100;
    const ddLimit = safetyCfg.accountDrawdownPercent ?? this.universalLimits.accountDrawdownPercent;
    if (accountDrawdown <= ddLimit) {
      return {
        shouldExit: true,
        exitReason: 'account_drawdown',
        details: `Account drawdown: ${accountDrawdown.toFixed(2)}% <= ${ddLimit}%`,
        confidence: 100,
      };
    }
  }

  // ─── SAFETY CHECK 3: Max hold timeout ───
  const maxHold = safetyCfg.maxHoldTimeMinutes ?? this.universalLimits.maxHoldTimeMinutes ?? 480;
  if (holdTimeMinutes >= maxHold) {
    return {
      shouldExit: true,
      exitReason: 'max_hold_timeout',
      details: `Max hold exceeded: ${holdTimeMinutes.toFixed(0)}min >= ${maxHold}min`,
      confidence: 100,
    };
  }

  // ─── SAFETY CHECK 4: Strategy invalidation conditions ───
  // These are strategy-specific "setup is no longer valid" exits (e.g., EMA cross reversal)
  if (contract.invalidationConditions && contract.invalidationConditions.length > 0 && context.indicators) {
    const invalidation = this.checkInvalidationConditions(

javascript
  updateTrailingStop(currentPrice, profitPercent, options = {}) {
    const cfg = this.trailConfig || {};
    if (!cfg.enabled) {
      return { updated: false, reason: 'trailing_disabled' };
    }

    const profitPct = profitPercent * 100;
    const maxProfitPct = this.state.maxProfitPercent || 0;

    // ─── Activation gate ───
    if (maxProfitPct < (cfg.minActivationPercent || 0.5)) {
      return { updated: false, reason: 'insufficient_profit_for_trail' };
    }

    if (!this.state.trailingActive) {
      this.state.trailingActive = true;
      this.log(`Trail armed at ${maxProfitPct.toFixed(2)}% peak profit`, 'info');
    }

    // ─── Base trail distance from ATR ───
    const atr = options.atr || 0;
    const rsi = options.rsi || 50;
    const trend = options.trend || 'sideways';
    const price = currentPrice;

    const atrPercent = (atr && price > 0) ? (atr / price) * 100 : 1.0;  // fallback 1% if no ATR
    let trailPercent = atrPercent * (cfg.atrMultiplier || 2.0);

    // ─── Trend widening (RSI-confirmed strong trends get wider trails) ───
    const isBullTrend = trend === 'bullish' || trend === 'uptrend' || trend === 'trending_up';
    const isBearTrend = trend === 'bearish' || trend === 'downtrend' || trend === 'trending_down';
    if (isBullTrend || isBearTrend) {
      const trendStrength = isBullTrend
        ? Math.max(0, (rsi - 50) / 50)
        : Math.max(0, (50 - rsi) / 50);
      const widenMax = cfg.trendWidenMultiplier || 1.5;
      trailPercent *= (1.0 + (widenMax - 1.0) * trendStrength);
    }

    // ─── Profit ratchet (tighten as max profit grows past threshold) ───
    const ratchetStart = cfg.profitRatchetThreshold || 3.0;
    if (maxProfitPct > ratchetStart) {
      const ratchetFloor = cfg.profitRatchetFloor || 0.6;
      const ratchetRate = cfg.profitRatchetRate || 0.1;
      const ratchetFactor = Math.max(
        ratchetFloor,
        1.0 - (maxProfitPct - ratchetStart) * ratchetRate
      );
      trailPercent *= ratchetFactor;
    }

    // ─── Clamp ───
    const minTrail = cfg.minTrailPercent || 0.3;
    const maxTrail = cfg.maxTrailPercent || 3.0;
    trailPercent = Math.max(minTrail, Math.min(maxTrail, trailPercent));

    // ─── Calculate new stop level as % profit locked in ───
    // Stop is placed trailPercent BELOW the max profit reached
    const trailStopPercent = maxProfitPct - trailPercent;

    // Enforce fee buffer floor (never trail below fee threshold)
    const feeFloor = cfg.feeBufferPercent || 0.15;
    const effectiveStopPercent = Math.max(trailStopPercent, feeFloor);

    // ─── Convert to price and ratchet state.currentStop ───
    // state.currentStop is a PRICE (verified from line 282)
    // shouldExitPosition() naturally fires when currentPrice crosses currentStop
    let newStopPrice;
    if (this.state.direction === 'buy') {
      newStopPrice = this.state.entryPrice * (1 + effectiveStopPercent / 100);
      // Only ratchet UP — never lower the stop
      if (this.state.currentStop === null || newStopPrice > this.state.currentStop) {
        const oldStop = this.state.currentStop;
        this.state.currentStop = newStopPrice;
        this.log(`Trail ratchet: ${oldStop?.toFixed(2) || 'null'} → ${newStopPrice.toFixed(2)} (${trailPercent.toFixed(2)}% trail, ${effectiveStopPercent.toFixed(2)}% locked)`, 'debug');
        return { updated: true, oldStop, newStop: newStopPrice, trailDistance: trailPercent };
      }
    } else {
      newStopPrice = this.state.entryPrice * (1 - effectiveStopPercent / 100);
      // Only ratchet DOWN for shorts
      if (this.state.currentStop === null || newStopPrice < this.state.currentStop) {
        const oldStop = this.state.currentStop;
        this.state.currentStop = newStopPrice;
        this.log(`Trail ratchet (short): ${oldStop?.toFixed(2) || 'null'} → ${newStopPrice.toFixed(2)}`, 'debug');
        return { updated: true, oldStop, newStop: newStopPrice, trailDistance: trailPercent };
      }
    }

    return { updated: false, reason: 'no_improvement' };
  }

Assessed architecture viability despite GPU downgrade constraints
Assessed architecture viability despite GPU downgrade constraints
That's actually fine for the architecture I proposed. Here's why the CPU downgrade doesn't break it:

What needs GPU (not in this plan):

Running a local LLM for chat (deepseek-coder, codellama) — slow on CPU, 5-15 tokens/sec, agentic loops become painful
What runs fine on CPU:

nomic-embed-text embeddings — it's a 137M param model, runs at 50-200ms per chunk on CPU. Indexing your whole repo (~2000 chunks) takes 2-7 minutes one-time, then only changed files on re-index. Query-time embedding is ~100ms. Completely fine.
LanceDB vector search — CPU-native, millisecond queries on 100K+ chunks. Never needed GPU.
Mercury-2 API calls — all the actual LLM heavy lifting happens on Inception Labs' servers, not yours. Your VPS is just shuttling retrieved context TO Mercury.
The architecture flow on CPU:

Query comes in
  → embed query locally (CPU, ~100ms)
  → LanceDB similarity search (CPU, ~10ms)
  → assemble top-K chunks into prompt
  → HTTP POST to Mercury-2 API (network, Mercury does the thinking)
  → parse response, handle any tool calls
  → if tool call: grep/read locally (CPU, instant)
  → loop back to Mercury
  → final answer
Mercury-2 is doing all the LLM work. Your VPS is a smart librarian that picks the right books and sends them to the expert. CPU handles librarian duties fine.

The only thing you'd lose on CPU: the option to run a LOCAL fallback LLM (Ollama with codellama/deepseek) if Mercury-2 goes down or you want to keep queries fully private. On CPU that fallback would be slow enough to be impractical. If Mercury-2 uptime is reliable, you don't need the fallback anyway.

Questions before I write anything:

Why the GPU → CPU downgrade? Cost? Underutilization? If it's cost and the difference is significant, CPU is fine for this. If you were planning to run local LLMs eventually, that plan dies on CPU.
What does the TRAI brain need Mercury for specifically? Real-time pattern scoring during trades? Post-trade analysis? Strategy generation? The latency budget matters — real-time needs sub-second, post-trade can tolerate 5-10 seconds.
Confirm Ollama is currently running on the VPS (for embeddings). If not, we install just that one model (ollama pull nomic-embed-text, ~270MB, CPU-friendly).

Identified beginner-friendly syntax question, prepared concise explanation
Identified beginner-friendly syntax question, prepared concise explanation
&& means "AND" — both sides have to be true for the whole thing to be true.

In decision.exitSize && decision.exitSize > 0 && decision.exitSize < 1, JavaScript reads it left to right and ALL three must pass:

decision.exitSize exists (not null/undefined/zero)
AND it's greater than 0
AND it's less than 1
If ANY one fails, the whole thing is false and isPartialClose becomes false.

With MPM sending exitSize = 250:

250 exists ✓
250 > 0 ✓
250 < 1 ✗ ← fails here
Whole expression = false. Partial close never triggers. Full position gets closed instead.

The other common one you'll see is || which means "OR" — only one side needs to be true. And ! means "NOT" — flips true/false.

Evaluated unit-agnostic fraction approach versus architectural refactoring needs
Evaluated unit-agnostic fraction approach versus architectural refactoring needs
Only Option A — the fraction — validates to that end state. Here's why.

The unit problem across asset classes:

Stocks: position is shares (e.g., 50 shares of TSLA) or dollars (e.g., $5,000 of TSLA)
Crypto: position is coin units (e.g., 0.0234 BTC)
Options: position is contracts (e.g., 3 SPY puts, each contract = 100 underlying)
If MPM returns exitSize = 250 (meaning $250), that's meaningful for stocks, meaningless for crypto (250 BTC? 250 satoshis?), and wrong for options (250 contracts would be a $2.5M notional position). OrderExecutor would have to ask "what asset is this trade on?" and branch into three different unit interpretations. Every new asset class adds another branch. Every broker adapter has to know MPM's unit conventions. Brittle.

If MPM returns exitSize = 0.5 (meaning "half"), that's universal. "Half of whatever you're holding" means the same thing for 50 TSLA shares, 0.0234 BTC, or 3 SPY puts. Each broker adapter just does newSize = currentSize * 0.5 in its native units and rounds to the nearest allowed increment (share, satoshi, contract). MPM stays asset-blind. That's the contract that scales.

The deeper problem you're actually pointing at:

Even with the fraction fix, MPM as it exists today can't handle crypto + options + stocks firing at once. Look at this:

run-empire-v2.js:610 — this.maxProfitManager = new MaxProfitManager(); — one instance, singleton

core/MaxProfitManager.js:170 — this.state = { active: false, entryPrice: 0, direction: null, ... } — one position's state, at a time

core/TradingLoop.js:170 — if (this.ctx.maxProfitManager?.state?.active) — checks the SINGLE state, not a per-trade state

When a TSLA long is open and then BTC fires a buy and then SPY options fire a put, MPM can only track ONE of them. The other two positions exit via ECM safety checks only — no tier logic, no trail, no BE scale-out. The module that does 90% of the exit intelligence is blind to 2 out of 3 live positions.

The end-state answer: MPM needs to be per-trade, not per-system.

Three ways to do it:

Map of MPM instances keyed by tradeId — this.ctx.profitManagers = new Map(). When a trade opens, create an MPM instance, put it in the map. When it closes, remove it. TradingLoop iterates active trades and calls profitManagers.get(trade.id).update(...). Clean, preserves MPM's existing API, minimal refactor.
MPM holds an internal Map — MPM becomes a multi-position tracker. mpm.startTracking(tradeId, ...), mpm.update(tradeId, price, ...), mpm.closeTracking(tradeId). More invasive to MPM internals, but one instance to wire.
Stateless MPM functions — MPM becomes a library of pure functions. State lives on the trade object itself: trade.mpmState = { tiers: [...], maxProfitPercent, beScaleOutFired, ... }. Each candle calls MPM.update(trade, price, context) which reads+mutates trade.mpmState and returns a decision. The trade is the source of truth. Persists across restarts via whatever serializes trades.
My recommendation for the end state: option 1 (Map of instances). It's the smallest behavioral change, MPM's internal state logic stays exactly as-is, and it scales naturally. Option 3 is architecturally purer but requires rewriting every MPM method to take the trade as first argument. Option 2 is the worst of both worlds.

For tonight: fraction fix first, Map refactor second.

Fraction fix unblocks the single-position case so RSI+EMA can actually prove the architecture works with real P&L movement. Map refactor is a follow-up commit — maybe 40 lines across run-empire-v2.js, TradingLoop.js, and OrderExecutor.js, zero changes to MPM itself.

Order of operations:

Claudito traces MPM's return sites (the request from my last message)
Fraction fix lands, smoke tests
P&L should actually move this time — green or red, but meaningfully different from -$502
If green, commit and celebrate the first real unlock
Then Map-of-MPM-instances refactor to make the system multi-asset ready
Then PATCH 3 (wire DynamicPositionSizer) — which is also asset-agnostic via the fraction contract
Add ogz-meta/MULTI-ASSET-READINESS.md documenting what's done and what's left
One more thing worth surfacing before we touch code:

When you're running Kraken crypto + Alpaca stocks + someday Tastyworks options, each broker has its own position state. A single stateManager with a single balance number and a single position number doesn't model "$3,000 in TSLA long AND 0.02 BTC long AND 2 SPY puts" cleanly. That's a separate piece of architecture — the broker-aware state manager — and it's probably the biggest remaining piece after the MPM refactor. Not for tonight. But worth noting in ogz-meta/KNOWN-GAPS.md so you don't rediscover it cold in three weeks.

Validated normalized fractions and architected independent trade lifecycles
Validated normalized fractions and architected independent trade lifecycles
Normalized. That's the right word for what a fraction is — a value scaled to 0-1 that means the same thing regardless of what unit the underlying quantity is measured in. 0.5 means "half" whether the position is 50 shares, 0.0234 BTC, or 3 options contracts. And yes — your instinct is exactly right and it's the cleanest architecture possible.

You're extending the World A principle from strategies to trades. Let me make sure I have it:

Level 1 (already established): Each strategy has its own independent entry pipeline. RSI doesn't share logic with EMA doesn't share with MASR. Each evaluates its own signal, computes its own confidence, owns its own entry conditions.

Level 2 (what you're describing now): Each trade has its own independent exit pipeline. When RSI fires a long at $245, that trade is born with:

Its own MPM instance tracking its own tiers, trail state, BE scale-out flag
Its own snapshot of the config that was active at entry (tier targets, trail multipliers, scale-out fraction)
Its own context object (atr at entry, rsi at entry, volatility regime, strategy that birthed it)
Its own lifespan from birth to death — nothing external mutates its state
When EMA fires a BTC short two candles later, that trade is born with its OWN MPM instance, its OWN config snapshot, its OWN context. The two trades don't share anything. If a config update happens mid-flight (env var change, matrix sweep), in-flight trades keep riding their birth config. New trades born after the update get the new config.

Why this is the right architecture:

Multi-asset works natively. TSLA long + BTC long + SPY puts each have their own MPM. No singleton to fight over.
Config sweeping becomes deterministic. A backtest with TRAIL_ATR_MULTIPLIER=2.0 can't accidentally poison a trade that was supposed to run with 2.5. Each trade is a sealed environment.
Audit and replay become trivial. Every trade's exit lifecycle is fully reconstructable from the trade object itself. No "what was MPM's state at 14:23:07" — it's all on the trade.
Persistence across restarts works. Crash mid-trade, restart the bot, trade state rehydrates with its sealed config and its MPM picks up exactly where it left off. Today's singleton MPM loses all state on restart.
Tournament methodology cleanly extends to trades. You can run 20 Apex accounts where each account has its own config environment and trades from different environments never contaminate each other even if they're running on the same server.
What this looks like in code (conceptually, not a patch):

Trade object becomes:
{
  id: 'trade_abc',
  entryStrategy: 'RSI',
  entryPrice: 245.10,
  direction: 'long',

  // Sealed environment — snapshot at birth
  exitEnv: {
    beScaleOut: { enabled, triggerType, fraction: 0.5, ... },
    trail: { atrMultiplier: 2.0, minActivation: 0.5, ... },
    tiers: [...],
    universalSafety: { hardStop: -3.0, maxHold: 480 }
  },

    beScaleOutFired: true,
    tiersHit: [1],
    currentStop: 246.20,
    trailingActive: true,

}
Then:

MaxProfitManager becomes a library of pure functions that take (trade, currentPrice, context) and return an action, reading/writing trade.exitEnv and trade.exitState.
OR each trade gets its own MPM instance held in a Map keyed by trade.id.
The pure-function version is architecturally purer (the trade IS the state, MPM is just behavior) but requires rewriting MPM methods to take the trade as the first argument. The instance-per-trade version keeps MPM's internal code untouched and just changes how it's looked up.

Both are valid. Instance-per-trade is less invasive. Pure-function is more in line with the "everything is data on the trade object" idea you're describing.

My read on which matches your instinct better: pure-function, because you said "each specific thing has its own independent factors entries exits and env it lives in during its lifespan." That sentence is describing the trade itself as the thing, not MPM as the thing. If the trade is the thing, MPM should operate ON the trade, not own the trade. Pure functions make that explicit.

Cost of pure-function approach: MPM's ~1291 lines of class methods all need to change from this.state.X to trade.exitState.X and from this.config.X to trade.exitEnv.X. Mechanical refactor but large. ~200 small edits.

Cost of Map-of-instances: ~30 lines across run-empire-v2.js, TradingLoop.js, OrderExecutor.js (create/lookup/destroy). MPM itself untouched.

Examined mapping, memory, atomicity, and recording challenges systematically
Yes, every one of those is a real concern and I want to walk you through each honestly — including the stuff I don't know without reading more files.

1. Mapping — trade IDs
What I need to verify before building:

Where are trade IDs assigned? StateManager? OrderExecutor? Broker-side?
Are they unique across the bot's lifetime or just current session?
At what point in the BUY path does the trade have an ID? MPM.start() gets called at OrderExecutor.js:288, which is after the BUY fires but maybe before StateManager returns the trade object with its ID.
Risk if we get this wrong: we key MPM instances by an ID that doesn't exist yet, or that gets overwritten on the next trade. Map lookup fails, MPM falls back to "no tracking," trade exits via ECM safety only.

What I saw that makes me think it's OK: core/TradingLoop.js:164 already uses tradeId: activeTrade.id, so trades have .id when they're in activeTrades. But that doesn't tell me when the ID gets assigned during the BUY path. Claudito needs to read OrderExecutor's BUY path from line 280 to 320 and tell me exactly where the trade's ID becomes available. Without that, I'm speculating.

2. Memory leaks
Real. If we add to the Map on open and never remove on close, every trade ever opened stays in memory forever. In a 2-year backtest with 1400 trades, that's fine — tiny leak. In a live bot running for weeks across 20 Apex accounts, that's a slow death.

The rule has to be: every Map entry has exactly one creator (the BUY path) and two possible destroyers:

Full close path in OrderExecutor → profitManagers.delete(tradeId)
A periodic sweep that removes entries whose tradeId no longer appears in activeTrades (the dead-hand catch for edge cases)
Critical gotcha for partial closes: if MPM fires a BE scale-out and OrderExecutor closes 50%, the trade is STILL ACTIVE with 50% remaining. The MPM instance must NOT be deleted yet. Only delete when remainingSize hits 0 or the full close fires. Get this wrong and the runner half has no MPM tracking it.

3. Atomicity — the scary one
Here's the sequence with the current design:

1. TradingLoop: mpm.update(price, ctx)
2. MPM: mutates state.beScaleOutFired = true, state.remainingSize -= 250
3. MPM returns { action: 'exit_partial', exitSize: 0.5, ... }
4. TradingLoop: builds decision, breaks
5. OrderExecutor: stateManager.closePosition(price, true, partialSize, ...)
6. StateManager: updates balance, reduces position
7. BacktestRecorder: snapshots
The race window is between step 2 and step 6. If anything fails after step 2 but before step 6:

MPM already thinks the scale-out happened (beScaleOutFired = true, remainingSize reduced)
But the account still has the full position
Next candle, MPM sees profit on the "reduced" remainingSize, does different math than reality
State machine has diverged from actual account state
In backtest this is mostly OK because steps 2-6 run synchronously and nothing really fails. In live mode with Alpaca you WILL hit this — network hiccups, rate limits, partial fills, rejected orders.

The fix: two-phase commit. MPM's update() should return the action WITHOUT mutating its state. Then OrderExecutor executes the action. Only after success does a callback mutate MPM state.

Conceptually:

const result = mpm.evaluate(price, ctx);  // pure, no mutation
if (result.action === 'exit_partial') {
  const closeResult = await stateManager.closePosition(...);
  if (closeResult.success) {
    result.commit();  // now MPM mutates — beScaleOutFired = true, remainingSize -=
  }
  // on failure: no commit, MPM re-evaluates next candle with unchanged state
}
This is also exactly your instinct about each trade being a sealed environment. State changes get committed when the outside world agrees they happened. Until then MPM is just thinking out loud.

This is actually a bigger refactor than the Map-of-instances alone. MPM's current code mutates state eagerly inside update(). Changing to evaluate-then-commit touches every mutation site — BE scale-out, tier exits, trail ratchet, BE stop, everything.

4. Recording — the one I don't know
I don't know if BacktestRecorder supports partial closes today. I haven't read it. Before we build the Map refactor, Claudito needs to read core/BacktestRecorder.js and tell me:

Does it have a concept of "partial close" vs "full close"?
When a trade closes, does it record ONE exit event or can it record multiple?
